title: Chapter 13 — That The Principle Of Equality Naturally Divides The Americans Into A Number Of Small Private Circles
paragraphs: Americans Into A Number Of Small Private Circles

One might well suppose that the final consequence and necessary effect of democratic institutions is to lump together all the members of the community in private as well as in public life, and to force them all to live in common. But this would be to ascribe a very coarse and oppressive form to the equality that originates in democracy. No state of society or laws can make men so much alike that education, fortune, and tastes will not interpose some differences between them. And though different men may sometimes find it in their interest to combine for the same purposes, they will never make it their pleasure. They will therefore always tend to evade the provisions of legislation, whatever those may be. Departing in some respect from the circle in which they were meant to be bounded, they will set up, alongside the great political community, small private circles, united by the similarity of their conditions, habits, and manners.

In the United States the citizens have no sort of preeminence over one another. They owe each other no mutual obedience or respect. They all meet for the administration of justice, for the government of the State, and in general to deal with the affairs that concern their common welfare. But I never heard that attempts have been made to bring them all to follow the same amusements, or to enjoy themselves indiscriminately in the same places of recreation. The Americans, who mingle so readily in their political assemblies and courts of justice, are, on the contrary, in the habit of carefully separating into small distinct circles in order to enjoy by themselves the pleasures of private life. Each of them is willing to acknowledge all his fellow citizens as his equals, but he will receive only a very limited number of them among his friends or his guests. This seems to me quite natural. As the circle of public society is extended, one can expect the sphere of private interaction to contract. Far from supposing that the members of modern society will ultimately live in common, I am afraid they may end by forming nothing but small coteries.

Among aristocratic nations the different classes are like vast chambers from which it is impossible to get out and into which it is impossible to enter. These classes have no communication with each other, but within their enclosure men necessarily live in daily contact. Even if they would not naturally suit one another, the general conformity of a similar condition brings them closer together. But when neither law nor custom claims to establish frequent and habitual relations between particular men, their interaction arises from the accidental similarity of opinions and tastes. Hence private society becomes infinitely varied. In democracies, where the members of the community never differ much from each other, and naturally stand in such close proximity that they may all at any moment be merged into one general mass, numerous artificial and arbitrary distinctions spring up. By means of these, every man hopes to keep himself apart, lest he be carried away in the crowd against his will. This can never fail to happen. For human institutions may be changed, but not man. Whatever the general effort of a community to render its members equal and alike, the personal pride of individuals will always seek to rise above the line and to form somewhere an inequality to their own advantage.

In aristocracies men are separated from each other by lofty, fixed barriers; in democracies they are divided by a multitude of small and almost invisible threads, which are constantly broken or moved from place to place. Thus, whatever the progress of equality, in democratic nations a great number of small private communities will always be formed within the general enclosure of political society. But none of them will bear any resemblance in its manners to the highest class in aristocracies.
